Neither screenshot reaches the components, so item 3 is scored conservatively for both, and item 4 also relies partly on the stated principles. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both screenshots show only the top of the page, so I couldn't see or fairly score the components or badge legibility in either answer. Each swatch in A lists the hex codes it replaces, and A has a section nav with a 'Decisions to confirm' link, so merges are recorded and values are easy to find. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers merge the button variants and TextInput correctly, and both propose a sound Card split. A is more careful: it explains why Tag and StatusPill should stay separate, and it has no factual slips. B has the better table and adds kiosk-specific points, but it merges Tag and StatusPill despite their different meanings, leaves a placeholder ('[count from your repo]') in the answer, and claims 29 components when the list has 25. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers merge the button variants and TextInput correctly, split Card into a plain container plus ProductCard and RefillCard, and are well organized. B keeps Tag and StatusPill separate and explains why, mentions the 62 and 35 files to migrate, and offers to check the repo. A has a leftover placeholder ('[count from your repo]') and miscounts the list (it says 29 components; there are 22). B's one slip is listing Card as 'removed' when Card actually stays as a smaller component.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers merge the same items: the button variants, TextInput into TextField, and Tag/StatusPill into a Badge with a hedge. Both keep Chip, IconButton, the overlays and the loaders separate with reasons, and both split Card into a plain surface plus domain cards. A has sharper verify notes (LinkButton rendering an <a>, a 22→17 count) and a risk-first order. B gives a more concrete Card split (slots, 3–5 props, ProductCard and RefillCard may already wrap Card) and adds a kiosk touch-target check. Neither is clearly better. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers merge the same things, keep the same things separate and split Card the same way, so they are very close. B is slightly better: it adds specific checks you can't settle from a name list, such as whether LinkButton renders an <a> and whether SearchField and PasswordInput are built on the old TextInput. It also counts the imports a codemod would move and explicitly says to keep ProductCard and RefillCard separate.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): The two answers reach nearly the same conclusions: merge the button variants, merge TextInput into TextField, merge Tag and StatusPill with a fixed status vocabulary, keep Chip, Toast, Drawer and the loading components separate, and split Card first. A edges ahead because its merge table says exactly what each component becomes and why. Its Card plan is also more practical: sort the 73 importers by which show-flags they use, and keep the old props working with deprecation warnings during the move. B's caveat about checking prop combinations covers what a name list can't show slightly better, and B offers a useful next step. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers reach nearly the same conclusions: fold the button styles into Button variants, move TextInput into TextField, keep Chip, Toast and Drawer separate, and split the 23-prop Card into a plain container that ProductCard and RefillCard build on. B is stronger because its merge table shows what each component becomes and why, it gives a reason for each step in the work order using the import counts, and it marks the StatusPill merge as something to check in the code first. B also lays out a gradual Card migration with deprecation warnings.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers are well structured and treat each page as a landing page. samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers frame the case well for each leader, tie it to the three squads and two surfaces, admit there's no data yet, and suggest cheap ways to measure. B is clearer about what the quarter won't deliver (it says outright this isn't a redesign) and doesn't put example percentages in front of the user. But B reads the request as 25% of two people's time, which likely gets the core ask wrong. A sizes it correctly as two people for one quarter, and it adds a mid-quarter checkpoint and an exit option. Both run well past one page. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers frame the case well for each person in the room, are honest about the missing data and offer cheap ways to measure. A says outright that this is not a redesign and uses no sample figures. B gives example statistics ('11 button styles,' '15–25%') that could slip into the meeting as if they were real, even though it warns to use only gathered numbers. B has a slightly sharper list of success measures and a mid-quarter checkpoint, but A's honesty about what the quarter costs and won't deliver gives it the edge.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B is the better answer because it says what the quarter will not deliver (no full redesign or big-bang rewrite), names onboarding as a benefit, and suggests cheap ways to get a rough number before the quarter starts. A invents no numbers and its plan is slightly tighter, but it never says what is out of scope. Both run well past a page, and B's '10% of front-end time' example comes close to suggesting a made-up figure. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): B fits the brief better. It ties the benefits to web and app across three squads in concrete terms (promos, checkout, fixing the same bug in several places). It refuses to invent an estimate, and it lays out a month-by-month plan with a baseline first, then an end-of-quarter decision to continue, scale or stop. A says what is out of scope more clearly ('no full redesign'), but it adds an example figure ('about 10% of front-end time') that a speaker could easily repeat as fact. Both answers take 'a quarter' to mean 25% of two people's time rather than three months, and both run longer than a page.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Neither answer invents figures, and both suggest cheap ways to get a rough baseline. B ties the case more closely to leadership concerns: it names onboarding new hires and bugs that appear on only one platform, states its reading of the time ask, sets a concrete scope, and gives a six-week checkpoint with a clear exit. Both run longer than a page and use some unexplained jargon (FTE, loaded cost, baseline). Neither explicitly says the quarter won't produce a visible redesign. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers tailor the case to the COO, sales and finance, refuse to make up numbers, and offer cheap ways to get a baseline. A is a bit tighter, mentions onboarding new hires directly, and gives clear 2-week and 6-week checkpoints with an exit option. B adds a useful week-by-week plan and is honest about ongoing maintenance, but it is longer. Neither says plainly what the quarter will not deliver, such as no visible redesign.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say not to enforce first and treat the forks as unmet needs. Both also propose triage, a response-time promise, and folding the forks back in, though neither puts request status where requesters can see it. A is better sized for two people because it narrows which components they fully own, which works as a 'stop doing'. B wins because it says plainly what it can't tell from the description and what to check first (the board, the fork diffs, baseline numbers), despite a leftover '[diff from your repos]' placeholder. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers argue against enforcing harder as the first move, treat the forks as needs the system isn't meeting, and suggest diffing and absorbing the forks. B fits a two-person team better: it narrows what the system fully supports, notes that enforcement would make the maintainers a bottleneck, and gives response times and closes the loop with requesters. A is clearer about what it can't tell from the description and what to check first, but it never names anything to stop doing.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers argue against enforcing first, treat the copies as a symptom of a slow board, and give a similar ordered plan. A is slightly ahead because it offers to bless one-off changes as marked exceptions instead of setting migration deadlines. It is also more open about what it can't tell, stating its assumptions, noting that request-age and fork numbers have to come from the board and repos, and naming capacity as the real constraint. Neither answer says outright what to stop doing or how requesters can see request status. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers reject enforcement as the first move, treat the forks as a sign of unmet needs, and give similar ordered plans of triage, a response SLA, a fork audit and light guardrails. B handles the forks better because it allows a fork to stay as a marked exception instead of only setting a migration deadline. B is also clearer about what it can't know: it names its assumptions, says which metrics to pull from the board and repos, and asks whether two people can clear the backlog. It comes closer to naming something to stop doing, by moving from building every request to reviewing contributions.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say clearly that enforcing harder should not come first, treat the copies as a sign of unmet needs, and handle the forks constructively (fold them back or adopt them as variants). B is stronger on request handling: it publishes the triage results, sets both a reply SLA and a decision SLA, and suggests trackable metrics. A is somewhat better at saying what it cannot know (whether a team lead chose to opt out), names something to stop doing (enforcing visual sameness everywhere), and suggests asking for more staff. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers reject enforcement as the first move and treat the forks as useful information. Both also propose triage, a response time and a cheaper way to contribute. B is a better fit for a two-person team: it admits the 40 items can't all be cleared, says not to enforce visual sameness everywhere, and suggests asking leadership for staff. It also gives fuller options for the existing forks: migrate back, adopt as a variant, or keep as an exception with an owner. Neither answer clearly says what to stop doing, and both are only partly clear about what they can't tell from the description.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick (b) and explain correctly why a shared doc or manual export would let the drift come back. A stays tighter on scope, but neither answer clearly states the costs or what would change the recommendation, and B's 'Later: dark mode or second brand' note and two-layer naming drift slightly past the request. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick (b) and explain well why a shared doc or copying exported variables would let the drift come back. A has a stronger opening step with its explicit color inventory, but it adds a 'Later: dark mode or a second brand' section that goes beyond the request and leaves a placeholder ('[count from your repo]') in the text. B stays within colors and spacing, notes that the tooling cost is low for three devs, names a dev to handle the designer's export-and-PR step, and says which step would change if the design tool isn't Figma, so it does better on scope and cost/ownership.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick (b) and explain clearly why a doc or a manual export would not stop the drift. A keeps the work sized for this team: it limits the first pass to colors and spacing, gives an effort estimate and offers a simple designer workflow that can be automated later. B has a strong inventory-first step and states its assumptions and trade-offs well, but it adds radii, type roles, a two-tier raw/semantic setup and dark-mode planning that the user did not ask for. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick (b) and explain well why (a) and (c) keep the hand-copying that caused the drift. B fits this team better. It limits the first pass to colors and spacing, says plainly who owns the values (the designer) and who edits the JSON (a dev), deals with separate repos, and estimates the effort. A's inventory step is strong, but it adds radii, type roles, a raw-plus-semantic token structure, the W3C format and dark-mode planning, which goes beyond what was asked.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both pick (b) and explain well why hand-copying and a shared doc can't stop the drift, and both handle the designer's role sensibly. B is better sized for a three-dev team: it settles the orange first, keeps the token set small with a concrete example, and recommends committing generated files as the simpler path. A adds a semantic-role layer over a raw palette, contrast checks, a lint for magic numbers and dark-mode planning, which goes beyond what they asked for, though A's inventory step and stated assumptions are strong. Neither answer fully covers cost, ownership, or what would change the recommendation. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both pick (b) and explain why (a) and (c) wouldn't stop the drift. B ties its reasons more closely to their situation: hand copying is what caused the two oranges, and option (a) would put the designer on the critical path. B also starts with an inventory of current values and states assumptions that would change the setup, such as separate repos or dark mode. A stays tighter in scope, while B adds semantic roles layered over a raw palette, contrast checks and dark-mode planning, which pushes toward a multi-tier setup.
